posts.text:
POV: The Importance of Workforce Planning.

When we talk about Human Resources, many people think we only hire people, process payroll, and organize engagement activities. But our most strategic role is this: Making sure we have the RIGHT people, with the RIGHT skills, in the RIGHT place, at the RIGHT time. That is Workforce Planning.

And in today's world, where everything is changing fast - technology, skills, customer expectations - workforce planning is no longer optional. It is a business necessity.

Allow me to share 5 reasons why Workforce Planning is critical for us:
1. It Aligns People Strategy with Business Strategy.
We don't hire just because there's a vacancy. We hire because there is a business goal. If the company plans to expand next year, to open a new branch, or to automate a process, HR must already be preparing the talent today. Workforce planning makes sure our people plan supports our business plan.
2. It Helps Us Anticipate, Not Just React.
Without planning, we are always in firefighting mode - rush hiring, overtime, burnout. With planning, we can foresee gaps. Who will retire in the next 2 years? Which skills will become obsolete? Where will we lack manpower? When we anticipate, we can prepare, train, and upskill - before the gap hurts operations.
3. It Optimizes Cost and Productivity.
Overstaffing is expensive. Understaffing is more expensive - it leads to fatigue, errors, poor customer service, and attrition. Workforce planning helps us get the right balance. We avoid unnecessary hiring costs while ensuring productivity is never compromised.
4. It Builds Future Leaders and Retains Talent.
Workforce planning is not just about numbers; it's about people. It allows us to identify high potentials, create succession plans, and build career paths. When employees see that we are investing in their growth for future roles, they stay. We don't just fill positions; we build futures.
5. It Makes Us Ready for Change and Crisis.
The pandemic taught us this. Companies with a workforce plan were able to adapt - they re-skilled, re-deployed, and re-organized quickly. Those without a plan struggled. In a VUCA world - Volatile, Uncertain, Complex, and Ambiguous - workforce planning is our resilience.

At the end of the day, business plans are just paper. It is PEOPLE who make it happen.
Machines can be bought. Technology can be copied. But a well-planned, well-prepared, and well-engaged workforce - that is our true competitive advantage.

So let us, in HR, continue to be strategic partners. Let us not just count heads, but make heads count.
Let us plan our workforce today, to secure our business tomorrow.

posts.text:
Stop building infrastructure as code with just one tool. If you're still choosing between Terraform, Pulumi, or CDK without understanding their real-world tradeoffs, you're setting yourself up for painful developer experience and deployment friction.

A team I know was stuck in a cycle where every cloud provider change required rewriting entire modules. They picked Terraform because it was the default choice in most DevOps hiring posts, but got burned by its declarative model. It worked fine for basic deployments, but when they needed to abstract over multiple regions or handle conditional logic, they found themselves fighting with HCL syntax.

The challenge was clear: Terraform's configuration language wasn't designed for complex workflows. Every change needed manual testing. They had to debug through the plan phase and make sure everything worked end-to-end instead of focusing on business logic.

Pulumi offered a different path. Their team picked Python or TypeScript as their first-class language instead of a DSL. They could leverage existing libraries, re-use code across projects, and even integrate with CI/CD pipelines more cleanly because Pulumi supports multiple languages natively. They moved from debugging HCL to running tests in their IDE.

But there's a catch — the learning curve for infrastructure as code became steeper when dealing with runtime dependencies. Pulumi requires you to think about infrastructure composition like any other app code, which is good but also means more concepts to master.

CDK took a different approach altogether. You write your infrastructure using familiar programming languages, making it feel like coding rather than configuration. It integrates well with existing developer workflows and teams already using frameworks like React or Node.js find it easier to adopt.

However, CDK comes with platform lock-in risks. AWS CDK only works with AWS resources natively, so moving away from AWS requires significant rework. They had to re-architect their entire stack when they expanded into GCP because the abstraction was too tight.

The resolution came from careful evaluation of their development workflow and team skill levels. Some teams thrived with Terraform's simplicity, others excelled using Pulumi’s flexibility, while a third group preferred CDK for its seamless integration.

What matters isn't which tool is "better," but how well each matches your team's experience, project complexity, and future plans. When your infrastruc

What would you try first on your team — or what's worked for you?

posts.text:
Reading me with the Comic makes it funnier. I promise. lol

Somewhere, a hiring manager is trying to order a senior engineer with free shipping and no assembly required.

“Does this one come with judgment?”
“Yes. Someone spent years helping them develop it.”
“Great. Can we remove that part from the invoice?”

Welcome to the pre-trained employee marketplace. Every candidate must arrive knowing the systems, understanding the customers and remembering an incident that happened before they joined.

Ideally, they caused it. That's the kind of ownership we're looking for.

A junior applicant offers to learn.

Unfortunately, learning requires someone who knows things to spend time with someone who doesn't. Finance has identified both participants as a cost.

So the vacancy stays open for nine months. Three senior people cover it. Two postpone their holidays. One starts answering recruiter messages while technically still in the meeting about retention.

Excellent. We have created another experienced candidate for the market.

The recruiter finally finds the perfect person at a competitor. They want a higher salary, a signing bonus and protected time to mentor junior staff.

Could we negotiate away that last bit? It sounds suspiciously like the thing we canceled to afford them.

Then comes the succession-planning workshop.

“Who takes over when our experts leave?”

Everyone studies the org chart as if a new employee might hatch from one of the boxes.

HR suggests developing people internally. The room reacts like someone has proposed making electricity at home with a bicycle.

Training needs real work, feedback and time from people who can teach. Cut all three and you may save this quarter's budget while bidding against everyone else for next year's seniors.

Back at the interview, the graduate has a question.

“Where did your current senior people get their first opportunity?”

A long silence.

“We're very proud of our competitors' graduate programs.”

posts.text:
It is a constant thought these days as every morning there seem to be new lay-offs, more down sizing and pivots into AI even as we see large scale push back and rejection of it. What if the source runs dry or gets cut off, say AI collapses or they make changes that do not work for your business, do we simply pivot back to hiring devs and try to revert these changes or is AI too integrated now to easily remove?

I am truly curious how the future of IT will look because we can not deny the capabilities of these models. However we also have to acknowledge the environmental and political impact these have had. If data centers remain a major political issue and see new legislation against them what will that do to AI as it is currently implemented. If data centers get shut down or curtailed what happens in that scenario, does pricing skyrocket or does service degrade? How would this impact revenue streams overall because we all know billions have been invested with no returns yet. How will shareholders react if they do not begin to see returns, what impact could they have overall?  

We also are seeing how AI can be used against big companies with the video game industry. Right now AI has enabled people to not only modify content easily they have gone on the completely reverse engineer games now from any era. They are jail breaking entire consoles and operating systems with ease essentially eliminating a major security these companies relied on. In turn Claude as changed its policies to ban this behavior but that obviously does not apply to opensource models and other alternatives not concerned with this. 

Much like piracy today there is no way to really regulate or stop this. The tech has been invented and given to the public there is no way to delete it or remove it once it is on the internet. How will companies navigate their software, IPs, and really anything they do online if they can not secure and protect them? We know cybersecurity is becoming a major concern now that AI is easily finding vulnerabilities in every way. If security can not be guaranteed what changes come to how we operate business? I really wonder just how much of this is being discussed and planned for across the market.

posts.text:
🚨 THE AMERICAN JOB MARKET IS DOING SOMETHING VERY STRANGE!
 
Companies aren't hiring many workers.
 
But they're not firing them either!
 
And that contradiction could have major implications for mortgage rates.
 
📉 Today's unemployment claims report showed just 189,000 Americans filing new claims, the lowest since July.
 
That's EIGHT consecutive weeks with claims at or below 200,000!
 
Sounds like a booming labor market, doesn't it?
 
Not necessarily.
 
📊 Employers have been adding an average of only about 68,000 jobs per month this year.
 
We're experiencing what economists call a "low-hire, low-fire" economy.
Businesses are holding on to their existing employees, but they're hesitant to expand their payrolls.
 
Here's why this matters for housing.
🏠 Tomorrow morning, we'll get the October employment report, one of the most important economic releases for the mortgage market.
 
A stronger-than-expected report could push Treasury yields and mortgage rates higher.
 
A weaker-than-expected report could help mortgage rates move lower, depending on the underlying details.
 
And remember, the Federal Reserve does NOT directly set mortgage rates!
 
Mortgage rates are heavily influenced by the bond market, which reacts to inflation, employment, and expectations for future economic growth.
 
💡 Low layoffs are encouraging, but they don't necessarily mean unemployed Americans are finding new jobs easily.
 
That's why tomorrow's numbers deserve so much attention.
 
I'll be watching the report and the mortgage-backed securities market to see how investors respond.
 
Do you think we're looking at a resilient labor market, or an economy that's slowly losing momentum?

posts.text:
Met someone last weekend. Six years of experience, real work, real skills. 

That’s the part nobody says out loud: hiring is broken on both sides. Candidates send 300 applications and hear nothing back. Recruiters get 1,000 applications for one role and can interview 8. It’s a buffet with a thousand dishes and a teaspoon. You don’t pick the best one. You pick whatever you can reach.

And here’s the real catch. “5 years of React” on a resume could mean years of building complex apps, or barely touching it. On paper, they look the same. The only place you get to prove the difference is the interview, and the interview never comes.

So we’re building VibeTwin, a twin trained on your real work. It talks to recruiters and their agents for you, and they can ask it real questions before the first call. Company agents talk to candidate twins. Humans meet when it’s already worth the hour.
Everybody is building software to interview candidates. We built the opposite: something that represents you.

What’s the most frustrating part of hiring right now, from whichever side you’re on?

Introduction At IBM Software, we transform client challenges into solutions. Building the worlds leading AI-powered, cloud-native products that shape the future of business and society. posts.text:
Some bad news I usually have to give founders: Your best candidate probably won’t see your job ad.

They’ll hear about the role from a friend (or a recruiter), and the conversation goes something like this:

“This startup is hiring a senior engineer.”
“Oh nice, what’s the role?”
“Uh... React, Python, AWS. 8+ years. Startup mindset.”
“I’m good, thanks.”

Here's the same job, with a better description:

“This Series B startup needs an engineer to get their inference costs under control. The AI bill grows every time they add a customer, and they want the cost cut in half without the product getting worse. You’d make the architecture calls, and it pays $180k to $240k plus equity.”

“Can you introduce us?”

Posting on a new job board won’t fix a JD that says nothing about the work.

If a friend can’t explain your role over a beer, rewrite it until they can.

posts.text:
Wrapping up my first term at WGU 🎓

Six months ago, I started my B.S. in Computer Science at Western Governors University. This week, I closed out my first term with 11 courses completed. Highlights included:

Prompt Engineering
Discrete Mathematics I & II
Computer Architecture
Java Frameworks & Backend Programming
Linux Foundations
Operating Systems
Intro to AI for Computer Scientists

What I enjoyed most was the range. I wrote LEGv8 assembly (a teaching subset of ARMv8) and studied how CPUs execute instructions, worked through OS internals and Linux, and built Spring-based Java backends. Coming from a TypeScript/React background, building a more complete picture from the hardware up has changed how I approach every project.

I've been able to keep this pace by setting weekly and daily goals, checking in with my Program Mentor each week, and building a knowledge base in Obsidian as I studied.

My second and final term is ahead, with Data Structures & Algorithms, Advanced AI/ML, and my capstone to round things out. I’m on track to graduate in April 2027.

I’m on the hunt for Summer 2027 software engineering internships and new grad roles. If your team is hiring, I’d love to connect.

posts.text:
LLMs are great at pulling data out of documents. They're also great at confidently making it up.

So I built PolicyLens to deal with that.

It reads insurance policy PDFs and uses an LLM to extract 10 structured fields: policy number, coverage limits, dates and so on. The catch: the model has to return a word-for-word quote from the document for every single value.

Before anything is saved, my code checks that each quote actually exists in the source text. If the evidence isn't there, that field's confidence is capped and it gets flagged. That catches fabricated values without paying for a second model call.

From there:
✅ High-confidence fields are accepted automatically
🔎 Everything else goes to a React review screen that shows the value, its confidence and the cited evidence side by side
🔁 The LLM layer is provider-agnostic (OpenAI, Anthropic or an offline mock), with Pydantic schema validation and one repair retry if the JSON comes back malformed

Biggest lesson: don't trust the model's output, verify it against something you control. A cheap string check beat a lot of clever prompting.

Stack: Python, FastAPI, React/Redux, PostgreSQL, Docker, GitHub Actions, 37 PyTest tests.
Code: https://lnkd.in/gMK8PiFH

posts.text:
HirePilot | Candidate Discovery Beyond Keyword Matching

100,000 candidate profiles. One job description. A ranked shortlist of 100 candidates.
For INDIA.RUNS - Track 01: Intelligent Candidate Discovery, I worked on HirePilot, an AI-powered candidate ranking platform designed to address a fundamental limitation in traditional hiring systems: relying on keyword matches to identify candidate relevance.

The objective was to build beyond conventional ATS filtering and evaluate candidates through a combination of contextual understanding and multiple independent signals.

What went into HirePilot
▪ Semantic matching: Sentence Transformers-based embeddings to evaluate contextual relevance between job descriptions and candidate profiles.
▪ Multi-signal scoring: Combining semantic similarity, technical skills, experience, education and behavioral signals into a weighted candidate score.
▪ Fraud detection: Identifying patterns such as skill stuffing, inconsistent career timelines and suspicious profile signals, with penalties applied during ranking.
▪ Explainable recommendations: Each shortlisted candidate receives a human-readable explanation alongside individual scoring dimensions.

Engineering the pipeline
The system uses React + TypeScript for the frontend and FastAPI for the backend, with a processing pipeline built around:
▪ JSONL streaming for memory-efficient handling of large candidate datasets.
▪ ORJSON parsing and batched embedding inference.
▪ CPU-level processing optimizations and single-pass scoring.
▪ Automated ranking and export of the Top 100 candidates with their scores and reasoning.

The submitted output contains a ranked shortlist with candidate identifiers, scores and explanations.

The interesting engineering problem was not simply generating a ranking. It was making that ranking contextual, multi-dimensional, explainable and computationally practical at scale.

This was a valuable opportunity to work on applied AI, information retrieval, ranking systems and performance engineering framed as a LeetCode Question.

posts.text:
At Future Food-Tech London, GLP-1 dominated the conversation.
 
The industry knew it was coming, but it significantly underestimated how quickly it would be adopted and how much impact it would have.
 
Lisa Finney and Callum Quigley, who attended the event, saw firsthand how fast the conversation flipped to what the next disruption might be, and whether teams would be ready for it. Their take is that readiness comes down to three leadership gaps.
 
🔹 Can you see far enough ahead for it to change this year’s budget?
🔹 Do you have leaders who anticipate consumer needs, or only react to them?
🔹 When a decision cuts across R&D, procurement, sustainability and finance, who owns it?
 
Some of these gaps are solved by hiring the right leaders. But even the best-prepared businesses won’t see every disruption coming, and when one lands, what counts is how quickly the leadership team can make decisions together and change course. That’s the work Deepsky, part of Miramar Global Group, does with executive teams:
 
https://lnkd.in/dRi9R5Aq

posts.text:
Oja Markets is hiring: Operations Associate & Community Manager

Full-time | Remote 

Oja is a prediction market platform where people trade on the outcome of real events: football results, elections, entertainment drama, tech launches, whatever the internet is arguing about this week.


We need someone who already knows what’s happening before it trends. You’ll turn those conversations into clear Yes/No markets, resolve them fairly, and keep our community talking.

What you’ll do

* Spot trending topics and upcoming events, then write them up as markets with sharp questions, firm deadlines, and resolution criteria nobody can argue with

* Resolve markets on time using sources that can be verified, keep a record of each outcome, and escalate anything disputed or ambiguous

* Run daily engagement on X, Instagram, and TikTok: reply to comments and DMs, start conversations around live markets, and bring Oja into relevant discussions without being annoying about it

* Keep a calendar of upcoming events with real prediction potential, and report on markets created, markets resolved, and what the community is responding to

* Pass user feedback back to the team so it changes the product


Who you are

* You follow football closely, from the big leagues to the transfer rumours, and you have opinions

* You keep up with Nigerian and global politics, entertainment, and pop culture

* You write clearly and can compress a messy debate into one unambiguous question

* You check facts before you publish and you care about getting a resolution right

* You work without being chased, juggle several things at once, and can react fast when news breaks

* You can be available to resolve time-sensitive markets, including during big weekend fixtures

Experience with prediction markets, sports platforms, or community management is a plus. So is having grown a social community for a startup or digital product.


How we’ll measure the job

Quality and relevance of markets created, accuracy and speed of resolutions, how quickly you act on live events, community response times, and your contribution to participation and growth on the platform.

How to apply

Send us: Your CV and a short introduction on your interest in sports, current affairs, and prediction markets

Five sample prediction-market questions based on recent or upcoming events, each with its possible outcomes and how you would resolve it

The sample questions are the real application. Make them good.

For enquiries, reach out to Talent(at)mindraytech.com

Ady Water merupakan perusahaan yang bergerak di bidang solusi pengolahan air (Water Treatment), penyediaan media filter air, serta sistem pengolahan air bersih dan air limbah.
Selama 14 tahun, Ady Water telah membangun reputasi dan jaringan bisnis yang luas dengan dukungan 7 kantor dan gudang di berbagai wilayah Indonesia. Ady Water telah dipercaya oleh berbagai pelanggan dan sektor strategis, termasuk PDAM, PLTU, perusahaan Oil & Gas, pertambangan, industri Food & Beverage (F&B), serta berbagai proyek dan event berskala nasional.

WE'RE HIRING: Tech Mentor at the Apple Developer Academy @BINUS, Bali
I’m looking for a senior iOS engineer who loves to teach as much as they love to build.
Every year, about 220 learners from across Indonesia and beyond join us in Bali for nine months of full-time, challenge-based learning. They research real needs, design, code, test and ship apps for real people. Our mentors work alongside them like a studio team, and the Tech mentor is at the heart of that.

What you’ll do
-Guide learner teams through the full journey of building an iOS app, from first idea to App Store quality
-Share your knowledge in Swift, SwiftUI and the wider Apple developer ecosystem
-Ask the right question at the right time, so learners find their own way
-Work with fellow mentors to shape the program and keep it current

What we’re looking for
-Deep, hands-on experience in iOS development and Swift, at a senior level
-A real passion for mentoring and sharing what you know
-Warmth, curiosity and the ability to collaborate across cultures
-Good command of the English language

What you’ll find here
A dynamic, multinational team: about a third of our mentors and 20% of our learners come from five continents. You’ll work in Bali, in a program built in partnership between Apple and BINUS University, with a competitive compensation package.

If you know someone who would be a great fit, or if that someone is you, please send me a message.
